claim: A new knockin mouse line was generated with super ecliptic pHluorin (SEP) inserted into the N-terminus of GRIA1, the gene encoding the GluA1 AMPAR subunit.
source: Using homologous recombination, we generated a mouse knockin line (C57BL/6J background) that inserts SEP into the N-terminus of GRIA1, the gene that encodes the GluA1 AMPAR subunit.
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of the mouse line using homologous recombination and provides details about the genetic modification.

claim: Homozygous SEP-GluA1 knockin mice are viable, breed well, and appear physiologically and behaviorally normal.
source: Homozygous knockin mice are viable, breed well, and appear to be physiologically and behaviorally normal (see below).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and refers to subsequent validation experiments.

claim: The SEP-GluA1 knockin line fluorescently labels all GluA1-containing AMPARs throughout the entire brain.
source: This approach fluorescently labels all GluA1-containing AMPARs in the mice (Figure 1a–c), enabling robust visualization of excitatory synapses throughout the entire brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides both textual description and refers to figures showing brain-wide expression.

claim: GluA1 mRNA and protein expression decreased in homozygous SEP-GluA1 knockin mice compared to wild type.
source: We did observe a decrease in GluA1 mRNA and protein expression in our homozygote knockin line compared to wild type (WT; Figure 1d–f), most likely due to decreased stability of the resulting mRNA.
evidence: The manuscript reports decreased expression with supporting data in Figure 1d-f and provides a mechanistic explanation.

claim: GluA1 expression in SEP-GluA1 knockin mice was reduced to 56.6% of WT in the postsynaptic density (PSD) and 44.4% of WT in total membrane protein levels (P2).
source: Using biochemical fractionation to isolate synapses from mouse hippocampal tissue, we observed reduced expression of GluA1 in the postsynaptic density (PSD, 56.6% of WT mice) and in total membrane protein levels (P2, 44.4% of WT mice; Figure 1e and f).
evidence: Specific quantitative measurements from biochemical fractionation experiments are provided.

claim: GluA2 and GluA3 subunit levels showed a trend of increase in SEP-GluA1 knockin mice, though not statistically significant.
source: In contrast, we observed a trend of increased levels of GluA2 (P2, 107.9% of WT mice; PSD, 115.8% of WT mice) and GluA3 (P2, 113.4% of WT mice; PSD, 125.6% of WT mice) subunits in knockin mice, although these changes were not significant (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: Quantitative measurements are provided with statistical assessment.

claim: There may be a small compensatory increase of GluA2/GluA3 in the knockin line as a result of decreased GluA1 expression.
source: These results suggest that there might be a small compensatory increase of GluA2/GluA3 in the knockin line as a result of decreased GluA1 expression.
evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of the observed trends in GluA2/GluA3 levels.

claim: SEP-GluA1 expression levels were consistent across brain regions (hippocampus, cortex, and cerebellum) in knockin mice.
source: Western blots of total lysates from either whole-brain or individual regions (hippocampus, cortex, and cerebellum) revealed that GluA1 expression levels were consistent across brain regions in knockin mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Western blot data from multiple brain regions is referenced.

claim: No differences in miniature EPSC amplitude, frequency, rise time, or decay tau were observed between WT and SEP-GluA1 knockin mice.
source: Quantification of amplitude, frequency, and kinetics of miniature EPSCs. No differences were observed in any electrophysiological parameters between WT and KI mice. N = 16 and 18 cells from WT and KI, respectively. Unpaired t-tests were used for all comparisons. Mean ± SEM. mEPSC amplitude: WT 9.43 ± 0.20, N = 16; KI 10.26 ± 0.51, N = 18; p>0.05. Frequency: WT 0.33 ± 0.02; KI 0.33 ± 0.03122; p>0.05. Rise time: WT 2.46 ± 0.040; KI 2.49 ± 0.07; p>0.05. Tau decay: WT 8.49 ± 0.18; KI 8.83 ± 0.36; p>0.05.
evidence: Detailed electrophysiological measurements with statistical comparisons are provided.

claim: No differences in EPSC rectification were observed between WT and SEP-GluA1 knockin mice.
source: No differences in rectification were observed between WT and KI mice. Rectification index is the negative slope of the IV curve (between –10 and –60 mV) divided by the positive slope (between +10 and + 50 mV). Mean ± SEM. WT: 1.32 ± 0.048, N = 12; KI: 1.33 ± 0.042, N = 16; p>0.05.
evidence: Rectification measurements with statistical comparison are provided.

claim: SEP-tagged GluA1 receptors were properly trafficked to the postsynaptic site and colocalized normally with PSD-95.
source: We also observed that SEP-tagged GluA1 receptors were properly trafficked to the postsynaptic site and colocalized normally with other postsynaptic proteins, such as PSD-95 (Figure 2f–h).
evidence: Colocalization data from imaging experiments is referenced.

claim: There was a highly significant correlation between SEP-GluA1 signal and immunofluorescence intensity of both PSD-95 and c-terminal GluA1 antibodies.
source: There was a highly significant correlation between SEP-GluA1 signal and immunofluorescence intensity of both PSD-95 and c-terminal GluA1 antibodies, indicating that all GluA1 receptors express SEP in our knockin mouse line (Figure 2g–i).
evidence: Correlation analysis between SEP-GluA1 and other synaptic markers is described.

claim: All GluA1 receptors express SEP in the knockin mouse line.
source: There was a highly significant correlation between SEP-GluA1 signal and immunofluorescence intensity of both PSD-95 and c-terminal GluA1 antibodies, indicating that all GluA1 receptors express SEP in our knockin mouse line (Figure 2g–i).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the correlation data between SEP and c-terminal GluA1 staining.

claim: SEP-GluA1 knockin neurons displayed bidirectional homeostatic plasticity comparable to WT neurons following bicuculline and TTX treatments.
source: As expected, WT neurons exhibited a significant reduction of surface AMPARs following bicuculline treatment and showed an elevation of surface GluA1 and GluA2 after TTX treatment. SEP-GluA1 knockin neurons displayed a similar bidirectional change of surface AMPARs following bicuculline and TTX treatments, indicating comparable homeostatic plasticity in SEP-GluA1 and WT mice.
evidence: Homeostatic plasticity experiments comparing WT and knockin neurons are described.

claim: GluA1 knockout mice show deficits in LTP.
source: To assess Hebbian plasticity, we compared the expression of LTP in WT and homozygous SEP-GluA1 littermates (Figure 3c–e) as GluA1 knockout mice show deficits in LTP (Zamanillo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to prior work.

claim: No differences in either induction or expression of LTP were observed between WT and SEP-GluA1 littermates.
source: We observed no differences in either induction or expression of LTP between WT and SEP-GluA1 littermates (Figure 3e).
evidence: LTP experiments comparing WT and knockin mice are described.

claim: The knockin labeling strategy does not impair synaptic transmission and plasticity.
source: Overall, these data strongly support that our knockin labeling strategy does not impair synaptic transmission and plasticity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the homeostatic plasticity and LTP experiments.

claim: No differences in locomotor activity were detected between WT and SEP-GluA1 mice.
source: We observed no differences in the time course or total number of beam breaks between WT and SEP-GluA1 mice (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: Behavioral testing data comparing locomotor activity is provided.

claim: No differences in anxiety levels were observed between WT and SEP-GluA1 mice in the elevated plus maze test.
source: We observed no differences in time spent in the open arms between WT and SEP-GluA1 mice (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: Anxiety testing data from elevated plus maze is provided.

claim: WT and SEP-GluA1 mice displayed a similar preference for the novel arm in the Y-maze spatial memory test.
source: WT and SEP-GluA1 mice displayed a similar preference for the novel arm (Figure 4e and f).
evidence: Spatial memory testing data from Y-maze is provided.

claim: The knockin labeling strategy does not impair behavior as SEP-GluA1 mice display comparable locomotion, anxiety, and short-term memory to WT animals.
source: Overall, these data strongly support that our knockin labeling strategy does not impair behavior as SEP-GluA1 mice display comparable locomotion, anxiety, and short-term memory to WT animals.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the battery of behavioral tests.

claim: There was a significant correlation between SEP-GluA1 fluorescence intensity and uncaging-evoked EPSC amplitude.
source: We found a significant correlation between SEP-GluA1 fluorescence intensity and uEPSC amplitude (Figure 5c), indicating that SEP fluorescent intensity can be used as a proxy for synaptic strength.
evidence: Correlation analysis between fluorescence and electrophysiological measurements is described.

claim: SEP fluorescent intensity can be used as a proxy for synaptic strength.
source: We found a significant correlation between SEP-GluA1 fluorescence intensity and uEPSC amplitude (Figure 5c), indicating that SEP fluorescent intensity can be used as a proxy for synaptic strength.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the correlation between SEP intensity and uEPSC amplitude.

claim: High-frequency pairing of glutamate uncaging with postsynaptic depolarization significantly increased uEPSC amplitude and SEP fluorescence in stimulated spines.
source: We found that this pairing stimulus significantly increased uEPSC amplitude and SEP fluorescence in stimulated spines (n = 10; p<0.01 relative to baseline, one-way ANOVA), consistent with induction of LTP, whereas spines that received only postsynaptic depolarization unpaired with glutamate uncaging did not display similar changes (n = 42 spines; Figure 5d–f).
evidence: LTP induction experiments with statistical analysis are described.

claim: Spines that received only postsynaptic depolarization unpaired with glutamate uncaging did not display changes in uEPSC amplitude or SEP fluorescence.
source: We found that this pairing stimulus significantly increased uEPSC amplitude and SEP fluorescence in stimulated spines (n = 10; p<0.01 relative to baseline, one-way ANOVA), consistent with induction of LTP, whereas spines that received only postsynaptic depolarization unpaired with glutamate uncaging did not display similar changes (n = 42 spines; Figure 5d–f).
evidence: Control experiments without pairing are described.

claim: The strong correlation between SEP-GluA1 intensity and uEPSC amplitude is observed in both potentiated and unpotentiated spines.
source: The strong correlation between SEP-GluA1 intensity and uEPSC amplitude is observed in both potentiated and unpotentiated spines, suggesting that the concentration of synaptic GluA1-containing AMPARs reflects functional synapse strength at baseline and following plasticity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Correlation analysis in different spine populations is described.

claim: The concentration of synaptic GluA1-containing AMPARs reflects functional synapse strength at baseline and following plasticity.
source: The strong correlation between SEP-GluA1 intensity and uEPSC amplitude is observed in both potentiated and unpotentiated spines, suggesting that the concentration of synaptic GluA1-containing AMPARs reflects functional synapse strength at baseline and following plasticity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the correlation data in different conditions.

claim: SEP-GluA1 signal recovered in two phases after photobleaching, with an initial exponential phase reaching 50% fluorescence recovery within 30 minutes.
source: We also found that the SEP-GluA1 signal recovered in two phases after photobleaching (Figure 6b). In the initial exponential phase (up to 30 min), SEP-GluA1 reaches a plateau at 50% fluorescence recovery.
evidence: FRAP experimental data showing recovery kinetics is described.

claim: About half of the GluA1-containing AMPARs at the spines are part of the mobile fraction and readily available to be exchanged with AMPAR pools outside the spine.
source: This result suggests that about half of the GluA1-containing AMPARs at the spines are part of the mobile fraction and, therefore, readily available to be exchanged with AMPAR pools outside the spine.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the 50% recovery plateau in FRAP experiments.

claim: The timeline for mobile spine AMPAR exchange in cultured neurons has ranged from 5 min to periods longer than 15 min depending on experimental conditions.
source: The timeline for mobile spine AMPAR exchange in cultured neurons has ranged from 5 min to periods longer than 15 min depending on the experimental conditions (Ashby et al., 2006; Fang et al., 2021; Frischknecht et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2009; Sharma et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: In the intact brain, mobile AMPARs are exchanged after 30 min.
source: However, in the intact brain, the mobile AMPARs are exchanged after 30 min (Chen et al., 2021), in agreement with our observations.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work and compared to current observations.

claim: The second phase of FRAP represents a full recovery of SEP-GluA1 signal, indicating complete turnover of synaptic GluA1-containing AMPARs in vivo within hours after photobleaching.
source: The second phase at later time points represents a full recovery of SEP-GluA1 signal, indicating a complete turnover of synaptic GluA1-containing AMPARs in vivo within hours after photobleaching.
evidence: FRAP data showing long-term recovery is described.

claim: The timescale of complete AMPAR turnover is supported by previous observations establishing a similar time course between synaptic AMPAR remodeling and AMPAR metabolic half-life (~18 hr for GluA1 subunit) in neuronal cultures.
source: The timescale presented in this study is supported by previous observations that establish a similar time course between synaptic AMPAR remodeling and AMPAR metabolic half-life (~18 hr for GluA1 subunit) in neuronal cultures (Mammen et al., 1997; O'Brien et al., 1998).
evidence: This comparison to prior work is made with citations.

claim: The same individual bleached and unbleached synapses can be tracked longitudinally over several imaging sessions across consecutive days.
source: In addition, these results demonstrate that we can track the same individual bleached and unbleached synapses longitudinally over several imaging sessions across consecutive days (Figure 6a and c).
evidence: Longitudinal imaging data is referenced.

claim: This is the first time that endogenous AMPAR recycling has been studied in vivo for up to 24 hr.
source: This is the first time that endogenous AMPAR recycling has been studied in vivo for up to 24 hr, providing valuable insights into basal AMPAR turnover dynamics in the intact brain and supporting that these tools can be used to longitudinally track synapse strength.
evidence: This claim of novelty is stated directly.

claim: SEP-GluA1-containing synapses are mobile and present similar dynamics as other in vitro and in vivo systems.
source: Overall, these results confirm that SEP-GluA1-containing synapses are mobile and present similar dynamics as other in vitro and in vivo systems, supporting that our knockin labeling strategy does not perturb normal synaptic dynamics or function.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from FRAP experiments and comparison to prior work.

claim: 78% of automatically detected dendritic spines contained a SEP-GluA1 synapse.
source: Enrichment of SEP-GluA1 in spine heads was readily apparent (Figure 7c) as 78% of dendritic spines (visualized using a sparse tdTomato cell fill) contained a SEP-GluA1 synapse, defined as edge-to-edge separation of red spines and green puncta <0.25 μm (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of spine-synapse overlap is provided.

claim: The overlap between spines and SEP-GluA1 synapses occurred at a substantially higher rate than chance.
source: This overlap occurred at a substantially higher rate than chance as the distance between spines (magenta channel) and their nearest SEP-GluA1 neighbor (green channel) significantly increased when the magenta channel was rotated either 90, 180, or 270° relative to green (Figure 7d).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing actual overlap to rotated controls is described.

claim: SEP-GluA1 synapses were detected at a uniform rate across depth within layer 1 of barrel cortex, up to 100 μm below the pial surface.
source: SEP-GluA1 synapses were detected at a uniform rate across depth within layer 1 (L1) of barrel cortex, up to 100 μm below the pial surface (Figure 7e).
evidence: Depth-dependent synapse detection data is referenced.

claim: The automatic synapse detection algorithm achieved 80.8% agreement with human annotated synapses, with an 8.2% false-positive rate and an 11.0% false-negative rate.
source: Using the same threshold for defining overlap of 50% shared voxels (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1), we found 80.8% agreement between automatic and human annotated synapses (green dashed ovals in Figure 7f), with an 8.2% false-positive rate (automatic detection without an overlapping human annotation; white X in Figure 7f) and an 11.0% rate of false negative (human annotation without overlapping automatic detection, magenta dashed ovals in Figure 7f and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative validation of the algorithm against human annotations is provided.

claim: The accuracy rates of the automatic detection algorithm are slightly better than the rate of agreement between two expert humans annotating the same volume (72.3% agreement).
source: These accuracy rates are slightly better than the rate of agreement between two expert humans annotating the same volume (72.3% agreement).
evidence: Comparison between algorithm performance and inter-rater reliability is provided.

claim: Ground truth for synapse detection showed a true-positive rate of 75.6%, a 13.1% false-positive rate, and an 11.3% false-negative rate when comparing SEP-GluA1 and Homer puncta.
source: We found a true-positive rate of 75.6% (overlap of SEP-GluA1 and Homer), a 13.1% false-positive rate (SEP detected without Homer overlap), and an 11.3% false-negative rate (Homer detected without SEP overlap; Figure 7—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Quantitative ground truth validation using immunohistochemistry is provided.

claim: The false-negative rate is likely an overestimate of error as this fraction could correspond to Homer-containing synapses that either do not contain detectable levels of the GluA1 subunit or are silent synapses that do not contain any AMPARs at all.
source: This false-negative rate is likely an overestimate of error as this fraction could correspond to Homer-containing synapses that either do not contain detectable levels of the GluA1 subunit (i.e., synapses where GluA2/3 heterodimers predominate) or are so-called silent synapses that do not contain any AMPARs at all.
evidence: This interpretation of the false-negative rate is based on knowledge of synapse composition.

claim: The resolution of the 2p microscope in the X and Y directions is 0.55 and 0.57 μm, respectively, compared to 2.50 μm in Z.
source: The resolution of our 2p microscope in the X and Y directions is 0.55 and 0.57 μm, respectively (full width at half maximum [FWHM] of reconstructed PSF), compared to 2.50 μm in Z, suggesting that our ability to accurately segment boundaries of individual synapses in XY is greater compared to segmentation in Z.
evidence: PSF measurements are provided to characterize microscope resolution.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of the C2 whisker induced a significant rightward shift in the distribution of SEP-GluA1 intensity in the C2 barrel, consistent with increased synaptic SEP-GluA1 levels from induction of LTP.
source: Whereas the unstimulated barrel displayed a stable distribution of SEP-GluA1 intensity over time, the C2 barrel that received mechanical whisker stimulation displayed a significant rightward shift in the distribution of SEP-GluA1 intensity, consistent with increased synaptic SEP-GluA1 levels from induction of LTP (Figure 8b–d).
evidence: Whisker stimulation experiments with quantitative analysis of SEP-GluA1 intensity changes are described.

claim: Whisker stimulation-induced potentiation manifested as an increase in the mean SEP-GluA1 intensity as well as a smaller but still significant increase in synapse size.
source: This potentiation manifested as an increase in the mean SEP-GluA1 intensity (Figure 8c) as well as a smaller but still significant increase in synapse size (Figure 8d).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of intensity and size changes are referenced.

claim: The number of detected synapses in both the stimulated and unstimulated barrels was stable over time.
source: The number of detected synapses in both the stimulated and unstimulated barrels was stable over time (Figure 8e), suggesting that the observed plasticity was not expressed via net spinogenesis or pruning, but rather by a net potentiation of existing synapses.
evidence: Synapse counting data over time is referenced.

claim: The observed plasticity following whisker stimulation was not expressed via net spinogenesis or pruning, but rather by a net potentiation of existing synapses.
source: The number of detected synapses in both the stimulated and unstimulated barrels was stable over time (Figure 8e), suggesting that the observed plasticity was not expressed via net spinogenesis or pruning, but rather by a net potentiation of existing synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the stable synapse counts over time.

claim: Previous work has shown that whisker stimulation can induce NMDA receptor-dependent LTP in layer 2/3 cells.
source: Previous work has shown that whisker stimulation can induce NMDA receptor-dependent LTP in layer 2/3 cells (Gambino et al., 2014; Holtmaat and Caroni, 2016; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: AMPARs mediate the majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the mammalian brain.
source: AMPARs mediate the majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the mammalian brain, and their regulation is regarded as a key mechanism underlying long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy that give rise to learning and memory (Huganir and Nicoll, 2013; Malinow and Malenka, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: AMPAR regulation is regarded as a key mechanism underlying long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy that give rise to learning and memory.
source: AMPARs mediate the majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the mammalian brain, and their regulation is regarded as a key mechanism underlying long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy that give rise to learning and memory (Huganir and Nicoll, 2013; Malinow and Malenka, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Long-term potentiation (LTP) is characterized by increased AMPAR trafficking to the postsynaptic membrane and associated spine enlargement, resulting in a long-lasting increase in synaptic efficacy.
source: Long-term potentiation (LTP) is characterized by increased AMPAR trafficking to the postsynaptic membrane and associated spine enlargement, which together result in a long-lasting increase in synaptic efficacy, whereas long-term depression (LTD) is characterized by removal of postsynaptic AMPARs, resulting in attenuated synaptic transmission (Anggono and Huganir, 2012; Nicoll, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Long-term depression (LTD) is characterized by removal of postsynaptic AMPARs, resulting in attenuated synaptic transmission.
source: Long-term potentiation (LTP) is characterized by increased AMPAR trafficking to the postsynaptic membrane and associated spine enlargement, which together result in a long-lasting increase in synaptic efficacy, whereas long-term depression (LTD) is characterized by removal of postsynaptic AMPARs, resulting in attenuated synaptic transmission (Anggono and Huganir, 2012; Nicoll, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Impaired regulation of synaptic plasticity is associated with human neurological and psychiatric disease.
source: Impaired regulation of synaptic plasticity is associated with human neurological and psychiatric disease (Berryer et al., 2013; Henley and Wilkinson, 2016; Volk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Super ecliptic pHluorin (SEP) is a pH-sensitive variant of GFP that fluoresces at neutral pH and is quenched at acidic pH.
source: To overcome this barrier, we developed a new knockin mouse line wherein the AMPAR GluA1 subunit is tagged with super ecliptic pHluorin (SEP), a pH-sensitive variant of GFP that fluoresces at neutral pH and is quenched at acidic pH (Miesenböck et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the original description of SEP.

claim: When coupled to the extracellular N-terminal domain of the AMPAR, the SEP tag reports the concentration of functional receptors at the cell surface.
source: When coupled to the extracellular N-terminal domain of the AMPAR, this SEP tag reports the concentration of functional receptors at the cell surface, as the fluorescence of receptors localized in acidic, internal compartments such as endosomes and Golgi is quenched.
evidence: This is explained based on the pH-sensitive properties of SEP.

claim: The AMPAR C-terminus is a region important for proper function and trafficking to the postsynaptic membrane.
source: Our genetic labeling strategy also avoids confounds arising from manipulation of the AMPAR C-terminus, a region important for proper function and trafficking to the postsynaptic membrane (Sheng et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Many groups have used overexpression of SEP-tagged AMPARs in neuronal culture to study AMPAR trafficking in vitro.
source: Many groups have used overexpression of SEP-tagged AMPARs in neuronal culture to study AMPAR trafficking in vitro (Araki et al., 2015; Ashby et al., 2004; Kopec et al., 2006; Makino and Malinow, 2009; Patterson et al., 2010; Roth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established practice with multiple citations.

claim: Previous work using overexpression of SEP-tagged AMPARs in vivo has provided valuable insights regarding the molecular mechanisms of behaviorally relevant plasticity.
source: In addition, previous work using overexpression of SEP-tagged AMPARs in vivo has provided valuable insights regarding the molecular mechanisms of behaviorally relevant plasticity (Diering et al., 2017; El-Boustani et al., 2018; Makino and Malinow, 2009; Miyamoto et al., 2021; Roth et al., 2020; Suresh and Dunaevsky, 2017; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2015), but these methods enable receptor visualization in only a sparse subset of cells and exogenous overexpression may result in protein mistargeting and dysregulation.
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Overexpression methods enable receptor visualization in only a sparse subset of cells and exogenous overexpression may result in protein mistargeting and dysregulation.
source: In addition, previous work using overexpression of SEP-tagged AMPARs in vivo has provided valuable insights regarding the molecular mechanisms of behaviorally relevant plasticity (Diering et al., 2017; El-Boustani et al., 2018; Makino and Malinow, 2009; Miyamoto et al., 2021; Roth et al., 2020; Suresh and Dunaevsky, 2017; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2015), but these methods enable receptor visualization in only a sparse subset of cells and exogenous overexpression may result in protein mistargeting and dysregulation.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of prior overexpression approaches.

claim: The novel genetic labeling strategy avoids confounds from overexpression, allowing visualization of endogenous AMPAR expression in a manner that does not impair synaptic function, plasticity, or behavior.
source: The novel genetic labeling strategy presented here avoids these confounds, allowing visualization of endogenous AMPAR expression in a manner that does not impair synaptic function, plasticity, or behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by the validation experiments described throughout the manuscript.

claim: The SEP-GluA1 knockin mouse is the first tool that enables longitudinal tracking of synaptic plasticity underlying behavior at brain-wide scale with single-synapse resolution.
source: Used in conjunction with in vivo 2p microscopy, this novel SEP-GluA1 knockin mouse is the first tool that enables longitudinal tracking of synaptic plasticity underlying behavior at brain-wide scale with single-synapse resolution.
evidence: This claim of novelty is stated directly.

claim: The sequence linking the SEP tag and AMPAR N-terminus is known to affect protein expression and proper postsynaptic targeting of the receptor.
source: The sequence linking the SEP tag and AMPAR N-terminus is known to affect protein expression and proper postsynaptic targeting of the receptor as previous attempts to fluorescently tag AMPARs at the N-terminus have been reported to result in impaired synaptic function (Díaz-Alonso and Nicoll, 2021; Díaz-Alonso et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: N-terminal linkers were lengthened and optimized to increase the flexibility of the SEP tag, thereby limiting disruption of GluA1 function.
source: However, in our experiments, N-terminal linkers were lengthened and optimized to increase the flexibility of the SEP tag, thereby limiting disruption of GluA1 function.
evidence: This describes the design strategy used in the current work.

claim: Spine size has been reported to be proportional to synaptic strength.
source: In addition, spine size has been reported to be proportional to synaptic strength (Matsuzaki et al., 2001), but this is at best an indirect readout of synaptic strength, and in certain conditions spine size and synapse strength are completely dissociated (Lee et al., 2012; Sdrulla and Linden, 2007; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: In certain conditions spine size and synapse strength are completely dissociated.
source: In addition, spine size has been reported to be proportional to synaptic strength (Matsuzaki et al., 2001), but this is at best an indirect readout of synaptic strength, and in certain conditions spine size and synapse strength are completely dissociated (Lee et al., 2012; Sdrulla and Linden, 2007; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The SEP-GluA1 line enables direct investigation of the molecular dynamics underlying synaptic plasticity at any scale, from super-resolution synaptic imaging in primary cultures to circuit-level analyses of plasticity in acute slices to brain region-wide imaging of synaptic strength in behaving animals.
source: This line enables direct investigation of the molecular dynamics underlying synaptic plasticity at any scale, from super-resolution synaptic imaging in primary cultures to circuit-level analyses of plasticity in acute slices to brain region-wide imaging of synaptic strength in behaving animals.
evidence: This describes the range of applications demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The genetic labeling strategy illuminates all GluA1-containing synapses throughout the brain, enabling investigation of synaptic plasticity from any brain region during any behavioral paradigm of interest.
source: As our genetic labeling strategy illuminates all GluA1-containing synapses throughout the brain, this line enables investigation of synaptic plasticity from any brain region during any behavioral paradigm of interest.
evidence: This describes the broad applicability of the tool.

claim: The SEP-GluA1 tool is compatible with any electrophysiological method or other fluorescence-based imaging approaches, such as neuronal activity sensors and genetic tagging of cell types of interest.
source: Further, this flexible tool is compatible with any electrophysiological method or other fluorescence-based imaging approaches, such as neuronal activity sensors (e.g., RCaMP) and genetic tagging of cell types of interest (e.g., engram cells, Cre-lines, etc.).
evidence: This describes the compatibility of the tool with other methods.

claim: By crossing the SEP-GluA1 knockin line with the Ai9 tdTomato reporter mouse and expressing Cre in a cell-type or neuronal circuit of interest, it is possible to specifically quantify changes in spine GluA1 expression of these neurons.
source: For example, by crossing the SEP-GluA1 knockin line with the Ai9 tdTomato reporter mouse and expressing Cre in a cell-type or neuronal circuit of interest, it is possible to specifically quantify changes in spine GluA1 expression of these neurons, as demonstrated in Figure 6 and Figure 7c and d.
evidence: This describes a specific application demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: Building upon insights gleaned by spine dynamics, the current approach additionally enables investigation of plasticity in existing synapses.
source: Building upon insights gleaned by spine dynamics, in which the formation and elimination of dendritic spines has been shown to be involved in several forms of learning (Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009; Xu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009), our approach additionally enables investigation of plasticity in existing synapses.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the current approach over prior spine imaging studies.

claim: Similar genetic labeling strategies have been used to investigate other synaptic proteins, such as PSD-95.
source: Recently, similar genetic labeling strategies have been used to investigate other synaptic proteins, such as PSD-95 (Cane et al., 2014; Fortin et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The current study is the first to engage labeling of endogenous receptors, which much more faithfully reports the direct physiological mechanisms of plasticity.
source: While overexpression of SEP-labeled AMPARs has been previously used to investigate behaviorally relevant plasticity (Diering et al., 2017; El-Boustani et al., 2018; Miyamoto et al., 2021; Roth et al., 2020; Suresh and Dunaevsky, 2017; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2015), the current study is the first to engage labeling of endogenous receptors, which much more faithfully reports the direct physiological mechanisms of plasticity.
evidence: This claim of novelty is stated directly with comparison to prior overexpression approaches.

claim: The tools presented enable automatic detection and segmentation of hundreds of thousands of fluorescently labeled AMPARs in vivo.
source: Finally, we present a suite of algorithms to automatically detect and segment hundreds of thousands of fluorescently labeled AMPARs in vivo, enabling longitudinal tracking of synaptic plasticity across entire brain regions in awake behaving mice.
evidence: This describes the computational tools developed in the study.

claim: The automatic synapse detection algorithm enables robust identification and segmentation of hundreds of thousands of SEP-GluA1 synapses in vivo, with accuracy at least comparable to expert human annotators, but with vastly increased speed and scale.
